QQQ.source: Yahoo Finance via yfinance (unofficial provider client)

interpretation.text:
QQQ’s 252-return DFA H=0.478 is near the independent, finite-variance reference 0.5. R²=0.956 measures fit only over scales 8–63. But short-scale (8–20) H=0.429 versus long-scale (25–63) H=0.660 means one straight-line exponent fits poorly: possibly crossover or a transient volatility shift, not one clean scaling law. DFA-1 of magnitudes, h_abs=0.733, contrasts stronger volatility clustering with near-0.5 signed returns—not tradable predictability.

H fell 0.018/0.022 over one/five observations. Its prior-only 30-observation standardized deviation is +0.017; overlapping windows prevent interpreting this as a significance test. From 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-11, H moved 0.520→0.478 and alpha 3.300→3.380.

Hill alpha=3.380 uses 1,000 returns (~four years), k=100 extremes, and x_min=0.02018 absolute log-return units. Conditional on a suitable tail model, lower/higher alpha means heavier/thinner fitted tails. Its idealized i.i.d. reference error, alpha/√k=0.338, understates uncertainty under dependence. The 5%/15% cutoffs give 3.593/3.039—not a confidence interval. Unchanged alpha can reflect new returns missing the top-k extremes, not static markets. These are uncertain descriptive estimates, not a crash forecast.

interpretation.text:

Short/long H=0.385/0.726 means one straight-line exponent fits poorly across scales 8–63: possibly crossover or a transient volatility shift, not one clean scaling law.

DFA-1 of return magnitudes gives h_abs=0.746: stronger magnitude persistence than near-0.5 signed returns, a descriptive volatility-clustering contrast, not tradable predictability.

The 5%/15% cutoffs give 3.297/2.574; this sensitivity is not a confidence interval. These are uncertain descriptive estimates, not a crash forecast.

NVDA.source: Yahoo Finance via yfinance (unofficial provider client)

interpretation.text:
NVDA’s 252-return DFA H rose from 0.404 on 2026-10-01 to 0.476 on 2026-11-11, near the ideal independent finite-variance reference, 0.5. R²=0.969 measures fit only across scales 8–63. H increased 0.013/0.048 over one/five observations. Its prior-only 30-observation standardized deviation is +3.09; overlapping windows prevent interpreting this as a significance test. DFA-1 of absolute returns gives H_abs=0.552: stronger magnitude persistence suggests volatility clustering, not tradable predictability.

Hill alpha fell from 3.028 to 2.909 across those dates. Conditional on a suitable absolute-return tail model, lower means heavier fitted tails; higher means thinner. Its 1,000-return window uses k=99 and x_min=0.04451 absolute log-return units. The idealized i.i.d. standard error, alpha/√k=0.292, understates uncertainty with dependence. The 5%/15% cutoffs give 3.339/2.862, not a confidence interval.

Alpha was unchanged November 10–11. Such plateaus are normal when new returns miss the top k extremes; they do not mean a static market. These are uncertain descriptive estimates, not a crash forecast.
